newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices ease on profit-taking, gold falls.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices ease on profit-taking, gold falls.

text.p: The coffee market came off the boil on Friday to close slightly lower as many speculators took profits after prices pushed to new 20-year highs.
Elsewhere, gold prices fell sharply while oil and grain prices rose. The Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures ended 0.92 point higher at 253.69 points.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery ended 0.55 cent a pound lower at 276.50 cents after earlier edging up as high as 280.00 cents -- a new life of contract high and the highest price since June 1977.

Coffee prices have soared since December amid shrinking stockpiles in both producer and consumer nations and concerns about lower supplies this year out of Colombia and possibly Brazil. Colombian domestic coffee prices hit record high on Friday after officials admitted export supplies were scarce.

But with the May coffee futures contract already up 41 cents or 17 percent for the week at Friday's high, many speculators decided to cash in profits before the weekend by selling futures contracts bought earlier at lower prices.
"It was part of a correction," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "It is still overdone on the upside and I expect we'll see a further correction on Monday."

Some concerns about tight coffee stocks at roasters eased after a report issued late on Thursday by the Green Coffee Association of New York, which said coffee stored in U.S. warehouses rose in April by 198,000 bags to 1,855,000 bags.
Each bag contains 132 pounds of coffee.

Also encouraging the profit-taking was a decision by the exchange to raised margins to trade coffee to $8,000 per contract for the most-active May and July contracts, adding selling pressure as traders closed out positions.
Margins are the good-faith deposits demanded by an exchange to guarantee futures contracts.
Elsewhere, gold prices ended sharply lower on the heels of Germany's plan to revalue gold reserves of its central bank. Gold for June delivery ended $3.50 an ounce lower at $344.90.

On Thursday, Germany's Finance Minister Theo Waigel said gold reserves of the Bundesbank would be revalued but no gold would be sold. The new valuation will help Germany qualify for European economic and monetary union, analysts said.
"Central banks tend to be net sellers these days and people, rightly or wrongly, jump to conclusions," said Greg Drury of Mitsui USA on trader views of future gold sales.
"If the market hears central bank and gold in the same sentence, it gets severely rattled," added Dinsa Mehta, Chase Manhattan's chief bullion dealer.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices rose sharply with many traders citing a change in the market's psychology after it shrugged off this week's news of large domestic oil supply and focused on international factors.
"Some feel that we now have a month where we will have strong gasoline prices, and this is the start," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products at Paribas Futures.

Mideast tensions, keying off a push by Turkish tanks and troops into northern Iraq in pursuit of Kurdish separatists, helped fuel nervous buying. But heavy buying by speculative fund investors and chart-watchers also was cited.
Crude oil for June delivery ended 82 cents a barrel higher at $22.12, while June gasoline rose 1.83 cents a gallon at 65.87 cents and June heating oil 1.99 cents at 58.47 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices closed higher on worries that dry weather in western Kansas may add stress to a crop already hit by a hard freeze last month. A snap import tender by Egypt for 50,000 tons of wheat also helped.
Wheat for May delivery ended up 4 cents a bushel at $3.87.
Soybean prices also ended higher, with soybeans for May delivery closing up 4-3/4 cents a bushel at $8.66-3/4.

Traders said early selling of soybeans was tied to a slowdown in soybean crushing at processors, who consumed 23.457 million bushels in the week ended May 14 against trade guesses that ran as high as 25.1 million.
But talk during the session of higher prices in Brazil, the main U.S. rival for soybean exports, was enough to turn the market around, analysts said.
"It's 100 percent dependent on what goes on with the Brazilian premiums and they were firming this morning," said Charlie Sernatinger at E.D. and F. Man International.
